title: US Midterms 2026: What a Congress Flip Would, and Would Not, Change for India
excerpt: Tariffs and H-1B rules rest mainly on presidential authority, so analysts expect scrutiny, not reversal, if Democrats take a chamber on November 3. The live restraint on the $100,000 H-1B fee is the courts, not Congress.
body:
• US voters decide control of Congress on Tuesday, November 3, with all 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats on the ballot.
  • Even if Democrats take a chamber, analysts say Trump's tariffs on India largely stay: they rest on executive powers under Sections 232 and 301 that bypass Congress.
  • H-1B tightening is also expected to continue either way, though the proposed $100,000 fee for new H-1B applications is currently blocked by two federal judges.
  • What a flip would change is scrutiny: hearings, investigations and pressure on trade policy, not the policies themselves, at least not quickly.

When Americans vote in the midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, India will be watching three things: tariffs, visas and negotiating leverage. The honest answer from analysts across the spectrum is that a change of control in Congress would change the politics around all three faster than it would change the policies.

Tariffs: the hardest thing for Congress to undo

A Democratic House could pass bills seeking to repeal tariffs, demand information from the administration and investigate the costs of trade restrictions, The Hindu BusinessLine noted in its analysis. But with a presidential veto in the way, such initiatives are unlikely to become law. The structural reason is that much of Trump's tariff regime does not run through Congress at all: duties imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 and Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 rest on delegated executive authority. After the Supreme Court rejected tariffs imposed under emergency powers law, the administration shifted further toward those provisions.

BusinessLine's conclusion is blunt: protectionism did not begin with this administration, and much of the Trump-era trade stance continued through the Biden presidency. There is, in its words, no strong reason to believe a Democratic House by itself benefits India. Indian exporters in textiles, pharmaceuticals, engineering goods and gems and jewellery would gain from reduced tensions, but existing tariffs would not automatically disappear with a flip.

H-1B and immigration: executive terrain

Immigration is the channel Indian professionals feel most directly, and it is also the one most firmly in executive hands. The tightening of H-1B norms and the suspension of PERM labor certification processing are administrative actions, and BusinessLine expects them to continue alongside a harder overall immigration line regardless of Tuesday's result. The sharpest current restraint on the administration is not Congress but the courts: the proposed $100,000 fee for new H-1B applications has been blocked by two federal judges on rulemaking grounds, a legal pause rather than a final resolution.

Foreign affairs expert Waiel Awwad, quoted by BusinessLine on Sunday, warned the mirror-image risk: a Republican victory that keeps unified control could mean a significant negative impact for India on H-1B visas, tariff pressure and immigration curbs, because the administration would read it as a mandate. A Democratic win, other analysts argue, would at minimum raise congressional scrutiny of restrictive measures and give skilled-worker advocates institutional allies.

Where a flip could still matter for India

Three softer channels could move even if the statutes do not. First, leverage: a weakened president facing a fixed end date in January 2029 gives trading partners reason to slow-walk concessions and wait. Second, energy: Democratic committees could press the administration on the costs of pressuring India over Russian oil purchases, giving New Delhi more room. Third, oversight of war powers: Awwad noted that if Trump loses the House, demands for a congressional vote before further military action against Iran would grow, which matters to India's energy security and its diaspora across the Gulf.

What to do with this

For Indian professionals in the US, nothing about visa status, fees or filing rules changes on Wednesday morning. The new Congress is seated in January, the H-1B fee remains blocked in court, and the administration's executive authorities survive any midterm outcome. The practical watchpoints are the court rulings on the fee, the pace of the India-US trade negotiation, and whether a new House majority uses its hearing calendar on tariffs in the first quarter of 2027.
